05 — Overview

How prompt assembly works, and why it is a builder rather than a string. Read this before you write code.

The request has a shape

Every request is a list of messages, and the first one is special:

[
  { "role": "system",  "content": "<who you are, what the rules are>" },
  { "role": "user",    "content": "<what the person asked>" },
  { "role": "assistant", ... },
  { "role": "tool", ... }
]

The system message is the only part of the conversation the user never wrote. It is your agent's identity plus whatever the project says about itself. Everything after it is the conversation.

Why a builder and not a format string

A single fmt.Sprintf works until the second thing wants to contribute. Then it becomes a format string with six placeholders and a strings.Join in the middle, and every new section edits the same function.

The interface is small:

type Contributor interface {
    Contribute(ctx context.Context) (string, error)
}

and the builder is a fold over the contributors. Chapter 09 adds skills by implementing this interface. It does not edit the loop, the provider, or the builder.

That is the point of the seam: later chapters add files, not edits.

The prefix must be stable

Providers cache the beginning of a request. If the prefix matches the previous request byte for byte, the computation is reused, and the response is cheaper and faster. If one character changes, the cache misses.

So the system message must contain nothing that varies between runs:

AllowedNot allowed
a constant base instructiona timestamp
file contentsa random session id
absolute file pathsmap iteration order
a fixed section orderthe current working directory as a sentence

Absolute paths are allowed because they are stable for a given workspace. Map iteration is not, which is the bug this chapter's stability case catches: two runs over the same files must produce the same bytes.

  run 1:  base + "## /w/AGENTS.md" + rules      ─┐
  run 2:  base + "## /w/AGENTS.md" + rules      ─┴─ cache hit
  run 3:  base + timestamp + rules              ─── cache miss

Discovery walks up, rendering runs down

A monorepo keeps rules at the root. A package adds its own. The agent should see both, and when they disagree, the closer file should win.

Order is how you express that without a merge algorithm:

  /repo/AGENTS.md          outer rules          rendered first
  /repo/pkg/AGENTS.md      package rules        rendered last

A model reading top to bottom reaches the most specific rule at the end, which is where a final instruction carries the most weight. Discovery therefore walks upward, then reverses before rendering.

  cwd = /repo/pkg
  walk up:  /repo/pkg/AGENTS.md   ✓
            /repo/AGENTS.md       ✓
            /AGENTS.md            (missing)
  reverse:  [/repo/AGENTS.md, /repo/pkg/AGENTS.md]

The walk is bounded, because a file at / is not project instructions.

Empty means absent

A file that exists and contains only whitespace is not an instruction. Rendering its heading produces this:

# Project instructions

## /repo/AGENTS.md
                              ← nothing

The model reads a heading with no content and concludes that instructions existed and were withheld. Dropping the section is more honest and keeps the prefix shorter.

The same rule applies to the whole section: if no file contributed anything, do not emit # Project instructions at all.

What assembly must not do

It must not touch the user's text. The prompt the person typed arrives at the model unchanged, as the second message. A wrapper added during assembly is a wrapper the user cannot see and cannot debug.

LayerMay changeMust not change
system messageassembled from contributorsnothing varies between runs
user messagenothingthe exact text the person typed

Where the real implementations go further

Concernpicrush
Context file discoverydocs/configuration.md, project trust firstinternal/discover/
Skill advertisingdescription-only until invokedinternal/skills/
Prompt cache controlprovider-specific cache markersprovider adapters

Two things they add that this chapter does not: a trust decision before loading project files, and per-contributor sizes. Both are policy; the seam is the same.
